title: Preventing
hook: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't arise

segments.voice: Yesterday: samma vayama, right effort, in four jobs: prevent, abandon, arouse, maintain.

Someone opens their phone to check the weather. Forty minutes later they're watching a stranger renovate a bathroom in another country, vaguely annoyed, and a little less fond of their own bathroom. Nobody decided any of that. It came in through the eyes, one tap at a time. Nobody broke down the door. It was simply left open. Today, the first of the four efforts: the one that works before anything goes wrong.
screen: `JUST CHECKING THE WEATHER.` → `FORTY MINUTES LATER.` → `THE DOOR WAS LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali word is saṃvara, restraint, and the suttas give it a specific picture: guarding the doors of the senses. Eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind: six doors. In the standard passage, when a practitioner sees a form with the eye, they don't grab at its signs and features, the details that set wanting or irritation going. Left unguarded, that door would let greedy and painful states pour in. So they guard the eye, the ear, and every other door. Notice what this doesn't say. It doesn't say shut your eyes, or never look at anything lovely. Seeing is fine. The guarding happens one step later, at the grab: the moment the mind zooms in, replays, wants more, or wants it gone. That's where the gatekeeper stands. The Dhammapada says it in one line, in Max Müller's words: "Restraint in the eye is good, good is restraint in the ear", and the verse runs on through every door. It's a quiet effort, and easy to overlook. Abandoning a mood once it's raging is hard work. Not letting it in costs very little, like fixing a slow leak instead of bailing out a flooded basement. And the doors now include a glowing rectangle, often built to keep the eyes on it.
screen: `SAṂVARA: RESTRAINT.` · `SIX DOORS OF THE SENSES.` · `GUARD AT THE GRAB, NOT THE GLANCE.` · `A SLOW LEAK, NOT A FLOOD.` · then, large: `GUARD THE GATE.`

segments.voice: With your eyes open and your gaze resting low, let things come into view without following them: a color, a shape, a sound from outside. Each time the mind starts to grab, to zoom in, judge or spin a story, let the thing simply be seen or heard; nothing has to be shut out, and nothing has to be chased.
Preventing. Saṃvara, restraint: guarding the sense doors so unhelpful states don't get in. The first of the four efforts.
Your line: guard the gate. The guard stands at the grab, not the glance. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Monastics practice sense restraint by keeping their gaze lowered on the alms round and avoiding entertainment; lay Buddhists often apply it on observance days and, today, to how they use screens and media.
